title: Simulations may explain how the Universe grew giant black holes so quickly
freshness: Published 2026-09-16; within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: Astronomers have struggled to explain how enormous black holes appeared so soon after the Big Bang. New simulations show a possible route in which unusually massive first stars collapse into large black-hole seeds that briefly grow extremely quickly, naturally producing objects similar to the mysterious little red dots seen by Webb.
whyItMatters: This gives scientists a plausible bridge between the first generations of stars and the surprisingly mature giant black holes Webb sees in the young Universe. It is a simulation result rather than direct proof, but it shows that such rapid growth may arise naturally in dense early environments.

exploreFurther.label: Nature: Overmassive black holes and little red dots naturally form in simulations

whatToExploreNext: Little red dots — compact, reddish objects found by Webb that may reveal an early, hidden growth phase of supermassive black holes.
body:
## A simulation of a head start

Giant black holes show up early. JWST finds them, and finds the compact red sources called little red dots, at times when a black hole that started stellar-sized and ate at a polite rate should not yet be enormous. A Nature paper published on 16 September 2026 reports a simulation in which the early universe grows those objects anyway. The route: unusually massive first stars collapse into large black-hole seeds, and those seeds then grow extremely quickly for a short time. The output looks like the little red dots.

Read the verb. This is a simulation. It is not a spectrum of a named object, and it is not a detection of a first-generation star. The notebook’s own summary says so, and it should keep saying so. The Nature paper is the only source attached to this note. There is no separate observatory release in the file to lean on.

## What the run is claiming, piece by piece

Piece one is the seed. If the first stars are unusually massive, the black holes they leave are large from the start. “Unusually” is doing the work of a whole set of assumptions about how those stars formed: less fine fragmentation, rapid accretion of the surrounding gas, a different cooling history in metal-free clouds. Those assumptions live inside the simulation. They are not new observations delivered by this paper.

Piece two is a brief episode of very fast growth. A seed buried in dense gas can accrete furiously until the gas is cleared or the supply thins. In that window the black hole gains mass at a rate that looks outrageous compared with a later, gas-poor galaxy. The window ends. You do not need the black hole to eat at that rate for a billion years. You need it for a short, early stretch.

Piece three is the resemblance. The simulated objects come out similar to little red dots: compact, red, and easier to explain if a lot of the light is tied to a growing black hole rather than to a mature galaxy of ordinary stars. Similarity is a comparison the authors are offering. It is not an identification of any particular dot.

## How this sits next to the black-hole-star note

Another note in this notebook, on MoM-BH*-1, is about an observed source that may be a black hole wrapped in a dense gas cocoon, and about the argument that little red dots could be that kind of object. This paper is a formation channel that could supply the black holes those dots might contain. The two results rhyme. They are not the same evidence. One is a spectrum and a fit. The other is a simulation that grows seeds and then looks at the mock population.

If the channel works, the “how did they get so big so fast” problem is less severe, because the seeds were never small and the growth spurt was front-loaded. If the first stars were not that massive, the channel does not open, and the problem stands. The paper’s contribution is to show that rapid growth can fall out of a dense early environment once you grant the heavy seeds. Granting them is the interpretive step. The early black holes JWST sees are the observational problem the step is meant to ease.

Treat the Nature article as the authority for what the simulation included and what it produced. Do not promote it to a discovery of heavy seeds in the sky. The dots remain the clue. This run is one way the clue can be produced without breaking the timeline.
